machine: darwin arm64, node v22.22.0, Apple M4

rows.input: I tried swapping chi for the standard library ServeMux now that it does methods and wildcards. Our metrics middleware reads the matched route pattern before the handler runs, and ServeMux only sets it on the request inside the handler, so every request got recorded under the path "unknown". Went back to chi.
rows.line: Swapping chi for the standard library ServeMux now that it does methods and wildcards. Our metrics middleware reads the matched route pattern before the handler runs

rows.input: I gave gRPC-Web a go for the dashboard so the browser could call the services through the gateway directly. The proxying works, but the dashboard's upload endpoint streams from the client, and gRPC-Web has no client streaming in browsers. Dropped it; the dashboard keeps its REST routes.
rows.line: I gave gRPC-Web a go for the dashboard so the browser could call the services through the gateway directly. The proxying works, but the dashboard's upload endpoint streams from the client

rows.input: Tried moving the rate limiter from Redis to an in-process token bucket on each replica to save the round trip. With three replicas behind the load balancer a client could get three times its quota, and a customer's burst test showed exactly that. Redis stays.
rows.line: Moving the rate limiter from Redis to an in-process token bucket on each replica to save the round trip. With three replicas behind the load balancer a client could get three times its quota

rows.input: I tried caching them with groupcache keyed on the API key's plan. It worked for reads, but the catalog includes per-customer prices, and two customers on the same plan with different negotiated prices got each other's numbers, so I took it out. A cache keyed on the account ID would work but has a much lower hit rate.
rows.line: Caching them with groupcache keyed on the API key's plan. It worked for reads, but the catalog includes per-customer prices

rows.input: I tried reloading the route table on SIGHUP. In-flight gRPC streams kept pointing at the old backend pools, and after a reload that removed a backend, those streams hung until their 10-minute timeout. I went back to rolling restarts, which drain connections first.
rows.line: Reloading the route table on SIGHUP. In-flight gRPC streams kept pointing at the old backend pools, and after a reload that removed a backend, those streams hung until their 10-minute timeout.

rows.input: I first raised GOGC to 200 and set GOMEMLIMIT to 80% of the pod limit, but the heap still grew by about 150 MB a day. A heap profile showed the cause: the per-route histogram gets a new label value for every raw path, so /v1/orders/123 and /v1/orders/124 are separate series. Recording the matched pattern instead of the raw path keeps the heap flat at 180 MB.
rows.line: I first raised GOGC to 200 and set GOMEMLIMIT to 80% of the pod limit, but the heap still grew by about 150 MB a day. A heap profile showed the cause

rows.input: The gateway-side retries made last week's checkout outage worse: when payments slowed down, every call went out three times and tripled the load on a service that was already struggling. Retries come out of the gateway; each client retries on its own with a budget.
rows.line: The gateway-side retries made last week's checkout outage worse: when payments slowed down, every call went out three times and tripled the load on a service that was already struggling.

rows.input: I tried storing the plant photos in SQLite as blobs so a backup is one file. The database grew past 600 MB for a heavy user and every sync diff had to read it, so the app took 8 seconds to open. Photos stay as files in the document directory.
rows.line: Storing the plant photos in SQLite as blobs so a backup is one file. The database grew past 600 MB for a heavy user and every sync diff had to read it, so the app took 8 seconds to open.

rows.input: fyi I had a go at the camera screen with react-native-vision-camera to get manual focus. Its native module needs a development build, and our testers all use Expo Go. Dropped it, expo-camera stays.
rows.line: I had a go at the camera screen with react-native-vision-camera to get manual focus. Its native module needs a development build, and our testers all use Expo Go. Dropped it, expo-camera stays.

rows.input: I tried WatermelonDB on a branch. It needs its own native SQLite adapter, which means a development build instead of Expo Go, and its sync protocol wants server endpoints we'd have to write for Supabase anyway. I went back to expo-sqlite with our sync code; nothing changed on main.
rows.line: I tried WatermelonDB on a branch. It needs its own native SQLite adapter, which means a development build instead of Expo Go

rows.input: I tried FlashList in place of FlatList with an estimated item size. The first render was faster, but the rows have variable heights from the notes preview, and FlashList kept jumping the scroll position when those rows measured differently from the estimate. I put FlatList back. The slow part is the thumbnail decoding; resizing thumbnails when a photo is saved would fix it.
rows.line: I tried FlashList in place of FlatList with an estimated item size. The first render was faster, but the rows have variable heights from the notes preview

rows.input: I tried that: worklets run on the UI thread, not a background thread, and they can't call expo-image-manipulator, so the resize never ran. I left resizing where it was; expo-image-manipulator already does the pixel work natively.
rows.line: I tried that: worklets run on the UI thread, not a background thread, and they can't call expo-image-manipulator, so the resize never ran. I left resizing where it was

rows.input: The sync kept creating duplicate journal entries when two phones edited offline. Adding a unique index on (plant_id, created_at) didn't help, the two phones write slightly different timestamps. Giving every entry a UUID made on the device and upserting on it fixed the duplicates.
rows.line: The sync kept creating duplicate journal entries when two phones edited offline. Adding a unique index on (plant_id, created_at) didn't help, the two phones write slightly different timestamps.

rows.input: Expo's push service has been dropping about 5% of watering reminders on Android, and we can't see why because the receipts only say they were handed to FCM. Reminders move to FCM directly from a Supabase edge function, where we get the error per device.
rows.line: Expo's push service has been dropping about 5% of watering reminders on Android, and we can't see why because the receipts only say they were handed to FCM.

rows.input: I tried django-cachalot to cache the ORM queries on the homepage. The invalidation is per table, and the articles table gets a write every few seconds from the view counter, so the cache was flushed constantly and the hit rate stayed near zero. Took it out.
rows.line: I tried django-cachalot to cache the ORM queries on the homepage. The invalidation is per table, and the articles table gets a write every few seconds from the view counter

rows.input: We had a go at generating AMP versions of the articles. Half our embeds (the election maps, the audio player) have no AMP equivalent, so those articles rendered with holes in them. Gave up on AMP.
rows.line: We had a go at generating AMP versions of the articles. Half our embeds (the election maps, the audio player) have no AMP equivalent, so those articles rendered with holes in them. Gave up on AMP.

rows.input: I tried Meilisearch for the archive search on staging. It's fast, but keeping 1.2 million articles in sync meant a second copy of every edit, and corrections took up to a minute to show in results, which the standards desk won't accept. Postgres full-text search stays.
rows.line: I tried Meilisearch for the archive search on staging. It's fast, but keeping 1.2 million articles in sync meant a second copy of every edit, and corrections took up to a minute to show in results

rows.input: I tried generating the renditions with pyvips instead of Pillow inside the Celery task. It was about three times faster locally, but the Celery image is Alpine-based and the libvips build there has no HEIC support, so photos from reporters' iPhones failed. I switched back to Pillow with pillow-heif; moving the task to a Debian-based image would let us retry pyvips.
rows.line: Generating the renditions with pyvips instead of Pillow inside the Celery task. It was about three times faster locally

rows.input: I tried streaming the article template. Django's template engine renders the whole template before the first byte anyway, and our middleware that adds the Content-Length and the ETag had to buffer the response, so the first byte came no earlier. I reverted it.
rows.line: Streaming the article template. Django's template engine renders the whole template before the first byte anyway

rows.input: The morning newsletter went out twice on some days. Setting the task's expires to an hour changed nothing, both copies still ran within seconds of each other. It was two beat processes after a deploy, the old pod kept running while the new one started, and a Redis lock around the beat scheduler fixed it.
rows.line: The morning newsletter went out twice on some days. Setting the task's expires to an hour changed nothing, both copies still ran within seconds of each other.

rows.input: Storing the bodies as raw HTML from TinyMCE has bitten us three times this year: pasted Word markup broke the mobile layout and one paste carried a script tag past the sanitizer. Article bodies move to structured blocks stored as JSON that the templates render.
rows.line: Storing the bodies as raw HTML from TinyMCE has bitten us three times this year: pasted Word markup broke the mobile layout and one paste carried a script tag past the sanitizer.

rows.input: I tried Hibernate Spatial for the depot queries instead of our jOOQ SQL. The generated queries didn't use the GiST index for the within-distance filter, so the nearest-depot lookup went from 3 ms to 400 ms. Back to jOOQ.
rows.line: I tried Hibernate Spatial for the depot queries instead of our jOOQ SQL. The generated queries didn't use the GiST index for the within-distance filter

rows.input: We tried the Kafka Streams DSL for the ETA calculation. Every restart rebuilt the state store from the changelog topic, about 25 minutes for the busy regions, and the ETAs were frozen the whole time. Dropped it for the plain consumer with its state in Redis.
rows.line: The Kafka Streams DSL for the ETA calculation. Every restart rebuilt the state store from the changelog topic, about 25 minutes for the busy regions, and the ETAs were frozen the whole time.

rows.input: I tried running the solver calls on virtual threads. The OR-Tools solver is native code behind JNI and pins the carrier thread for the whole solve, so with 16 solves in flight the other requests starved and p99 went to 4 s. I went back to coroutines on a bounded dispatcher; that stays.
rows.line: Running the solver calls on virtual threads. The OR-Tools solver is native code behind JNI and pins the carrier thread for the whole solve

rows.input: I tried warm-starting OR-Tools with the previous route as the initial solution. For a one-stop change it found a route in 300 ms, but with the time windows it often got stuck near the old solution and returned routes 12% longer than a cold solve. I removed the warm start; a small local repair around the changed stop might do better.
rows.line: I tried warm-starting OR-Tools with the previous route as the initial solution. For a one-stop change it found a route in 300 ms

rows.input: I tried a Caffeine cache for the matrix. The matrix for a big depot is 40 MB, and with the pod's 1 GB heap the cache evicted entries within minutes, so the hit rate stayed at 8% and GC pauses got longer. I removed it; the matrix service's own cache is doing more good.
rows.line: A Caffeine cache for the matrix. The matrix for a big depot is 40 MB, and with the pod's 1 GB heap the cache evicted entries within minutes

rows.input: Their GPS pings arrive out of order: the phones batch them when the signal drops. I first tried ordering by the Kafka record timestamp, but that's when the phone sent the batch, so pings in a batch still came out of order. Ordering by the fix time inside each ping and dropping pings older than the last one applied fixed the jumps.
rows.line: Ordering by the Kafka record timestamp, but that's when the phone sent the batch, so pings in a batch still came out of order.

rows.input: The WebSocket to the driver apps keeps dying: carriers drop idle connections after about 90 seconds and the phones reconnect in a storm when a cell tower hands over. Route updates move to FCM data messages, with the app pulling the full route when it gets one.
rows.line: The WebSocket to the driver apps keeps dying: carriers drop idle connections after about 90 seconds and the phones reconnect in a storm when a cell tower hands over.

rows.input: I tried generating the ticket PDFs inside the Worker with pdf-lib. With the fonts and the QR code it needs about 180 ms of CPU for a 6-ticket order, over the CPU limit on our plan, and big orders failed with a CPU exceeded error. Ticket PDFs are made by a queue consumer now.
rows.line: Generating the ticket PDFs inside the Worker with pdf-lib. With the fonts and the QR code it needs about 180 ms of CPU for a 6-ticket order, over the CPU limit on our plan

rows.input: We gave Turnstile a try on the checkout page to stop the scalper bots. The bots got past it about as often as people did, and some real buyers on older iPhones got stuck in a loop of challenges. Took it off checkout.
rows.line: We gave Turnstile a try on the checkout page to stop the scalper bots. The bots got past it about as often as people did, and some real buyers on older iPhones got stuck in a loop of challenges.

rows.input: I tried moving the seat holds from the Durable Object to KV with a TTL, to make them cheaper. KV writes take up to a minute to show up in other locations, so two buyers in different cities held the same seat. The holds are back in the event's Durable Object.
rows.line: Moving the seat holds from the Durable Object to KV with a TTL, to make them cheaper. KV writes take up to a minute to show up in other locations

rows.input: I tried prerendering the event pages at build time. With 3,000 events the build took 14 minutes and went over the CI build limit, and the ticket counts on the page were stale until the next build. I turned prerendering off for event pages; caching the rendered page for 30 seconds would get most of the speed.
rows.line: Prerendering the event pages at build time. With 3,000 events the build took 14 minutes and went over the CI build limit, and the ticket counts on the page were stale until the next build.

rows.input: I tried it: MailChannels ended its free sending for Workers, and without a paid account every send was rejected with an authentication error. I reverted to the Postmark API.
rows.line: I tried it: MailChannels ended its free sending for Workers, and without a paid account every send was rejected with an authentication error. I reverted to the Postmark API.

rows.input: Refunds were double-crediting some buyers. Wrapping the D1 writes in a batch didn't fix it; the Stripe webhook was delivered twice and both deliveries ran. Recording each event ID in a processed_events table and skipping the ones we've seen fixed it.
rows.line: Refunds were double-crediting some buyers. Wrapping the D1 writes in a batch didn't fix it; the Stripe webhook was delivered twice and both deliveries ran.

rows.input: Payment Elements has been trouble on checkout: the 3-D Secure pop-ups get blocked inside the in-app browsers of Instagram and TikTok, where a third of our buyers come from, and those payments time out. Checkout moves to Stripe's hosted Checkout page.
rows.line: Payment Elements has been trouble on checkout: the 3-D Secure pop-ups get blocked inside the in-app browsers of Instagram and TikTok, where a third of our buyers come from
